name: Felix Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a formwork gang on building sites: we put up the temporary moulds that hold concrete while it sets. My trade certificate helps, but what the younger crew trusts is that I can spot a weak brace before a pour. I sometimes use an AI tool to tidy a message to the site office, then read it twice before sending. My partner and I have grown children; our pay is at the low end for this trade, we have under a month saved, and there are few comparable jobs near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the gang that a quicker office note is fine if somebody still checks the pour plan. I already use AI now and then to clean up a message, not to decide how a shutter is braced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small saving on paperwork would not take the formwork away. Our savings are thin, though, and a stretch of rain or delayed site work already makes me count each shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the pours and double-check every brace against the drawings. In the first year I would use the same occasional AI drafting help for office messages, but keep the safety decisions with the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the next empty week, even if the AI itself is harmless here. A payslip with missing days is louder than any software story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check before a pour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The brace pins, the level of the panels and whether the access route is clear. If a panel shifts under wet concrete, I want to know we had eyes on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who notices a short week at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner notices when we delay the utility payment until Friday. We manage it, but there is hardly a reserve if two short weeks follow each other.

say: **Office AI** can shorten messages without deciding formwork safety.
I keep the **crew check** before every concrete pour.
think: Our **thin reserve** makes even ordinary short weeks stressful.
A small **paperwork saving** does not fix low pay or rain delays.
do: **Lead** the formwork gang and inspect braces before pours.
**Use** occasional AI drafting help for office messages while checking each message.
feel: **Anxious** about missing paid days, not about a small software tool.
S0.quote: A payslip with missing days is louder than any software story.
fieldNote: His **existing AI use** is limited to drafting messages and does not replace safety judgment.
His **baseline worry** comes from low pay and little savings during gaps between site shifts.

steps.text: Keep leading formwork pours and inspect braces

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the site office might schedule pours faster once software handles orders and checking. The gang still has to fit and strip the moulds safely, whatever the screen says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If managers expect fewer people to complete the same pour schedule, they may trim my gang’s paid days. I could learn a scheduling tool after seeing it work, but I cannot absorb many lost shifts or find another gang nearby quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the site engineer to show me a completed digital pour schedule and compare it against our last three jobs. In the first year I would take a funded, paid-time class on the scheduling tool if a real place is offered, and ask our union representative to challenge any unsafe cut in crew hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious because a timetable can turn into a pay cut without saying the words. I would rather learn the tool and argue from the actual pour records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mismatch would you look for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software might allow two hours to strip forms that took our gang four after heavy rain. I would mark the delay and explain the safety reason, not just say the plan is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the class yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have less than a month of bills put away, and the contractor benefits from the new schedule. I would need a funded place and paid hours to attend.

say: **Office schedules** may change faster than hands-on formwork on my building site.
Crews should use **pour records** to challenge unsafe deadlines.
think: Fewer **paid shifts** could follow if management shrinks the gang.
I can learn a **proven tool**, but cannot pay for training from our thin reserve.
do: **Compare** digital pour schedules with records from three recent jobs.
**Take** a funded scheduling class if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Raise** unsafe crew-hour cuts through the union representative.
feel: **Anxious** that a schedule could quietly reduce wages.
S1.quote: I am anxious because a timetable can turn into a pay cut without saying the words.
fieldNote: He is **steady** about technology: he wants to test the schedule against known pours first.
His **course condition** requires an actual funded place and paid work time.

steps.text: Take funded scheduling tool class if actual paid-time place opens
Ask union representative to challenge unsafe crew-hour cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the gang that AGI could take over the office plans by 2028, while robots able to build formwork arrive around 2031. Three years of hand work are useful, but I would not spend them pretending the later change cannot come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to catch a brace that looks sound on a drawing and moves under load. A capable robot could make that skill less marketable just when my partner and I need wages to support retirement; our small reserve would not carry us through a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the union’s proposal for a worker-led robot safety trial to the contractor and ask for paid training on inspecting machine-built forms. If a funded course place runs, I would attend; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local inspection job only if its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious and impatient for a real answer about training. I can learn by watching a safe trial, but an unpaid course would take food money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you make the robot trial prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a human inspector can see the load path, reach the brace and stop a pour before concrete arrives. I would not put the gang under a machine-built deck without those checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the inspection job is not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep taking formwork shifts while they exist and ask the union to push for a funded route into other site safety work. I would not resign on a rumour of an opening.

say: **2028 AGI** changes plans before capable site robots arrive around 2031.
Robot-built forms need a **human stop check** before concrete pours.
think: A capable **robot** could reduce demand for my formwork skill.
Our **thin savings** cannot carry a long search for other work.
do: **Propose** a worker-led robot safety trial through the union.
**Attend** a funded inspection course if a paid-time place runs.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only at bill-covering hours and pay.
feel: **Anxious** about wages and impatient for real training terms.
S2.quote: I can learn by watching a safe trial, but an unpaid course would take food money.
fieldNote: He accepts **robot trials** when a worker can inspect and stop the pour.
His **job plan** depends on a posted local opening with enough hours and pay.

steps.text: Propose union robot trial with visible load paths, brace access and stop before pouring
Attend funded robot inspection course if paid-time place runs
Apply for posted local inspection job if hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a 2031 AGI date gives us time to watch real equipment before it reaches the gang. Robots come around 2034, so the contractor has time to write proper inspection rules with the people who pour concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the inspection side if the course is built around a working trial, not a sales demonstration. But a few extra years do not fill our savings account by themselves, and the local job list is still short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union training group and contractor to set dates for a paid course and a site trial. If a funded place actually opens, I would complete it before 2034; in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted local inspection role only if its pay covers household bills, while keeping formwork shifts until an offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, with more room to test a sensible plan. I would use the time, though I need the wages during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the training meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who pays for the course, which shifts count as paid training and whether a passed inspection test qualifies me for an actual opening. I would want dates and names on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the formwork shifts after qualifying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An inspection certificate cannot pay our utilities bill on its own. I would move only after a local employer offers enough hours and wage.

say: **2031 AGI** allows trials before capable construction robots around 2034.
Crews need **inspection rules** shaped by real concrete pours.
think: I could learn **inspection** through a working trial.
A longer runway does not itself improve **savings** or local vacancies.
do: **Seek** dated paid-course and site-trial terms through the union.
**Complete** funded inspection training if a paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious**, though there is time to test a plan.
S3.quote: An inspection certificate cannot pay our utilities bill on its own.
fieldNote: His **conditional training** needs dates, funding, paid shifts and a real course place.
He would **keep working** until a local inspection offer pays enough to cover household bills.

steps.text: Seek written paid-course dates and job-qualification terms through union training group
Complete funded robot inspection training if paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection role if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children there is a decade before AGI and about three more years before capable construction robots in 2039. That is time to plan, provided the site still pays us through those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I may have done enough formwork, but I cannot promise to retire while we have less than a month of expenses saved. I would want an actual household budget and a pay offer before choosing shorter hours or a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present shifts and review our bills, savings and likely retirement spending with my partner each autumn. I would ask the union about a funded paid-time inspection course; if a place and a posted local job at bill-covering pay exist, I would take the course and apply during the first year after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about money more than the long timetable. A 2039 formwork robot leaves room to plan, but it does not put wages in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make retirement affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough dependable income for housing, food and healthcare without borrowing between payments. We would work that out from our own bills, not an age somebody else chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save more while you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we get steady full weeks again, we would put a fixed part of each extra shift into savings. I would not count the money already there as a new saving plan.

say: **2036 AGI** changes site plans before capable formwork robots arrive around 2039.
A decade helps only if **site wages** keep coming.
think: Our **retirement budget** is unknown while savings stay thin.
A **posted local offer** must pay the household bills before I change work.
do: **Keep** formwork shifts and review retirement costs with my partner yearly.
**Save** part of extra-shift pay if full weeks return.
**Train** and apply only if a funded place and bill-covering local job exist.
feel: **Anxious** about money despite a longer machine timetable.
S4.quote: A 2039 formwork robot leaves room to plan, but it does not put wages in our account.
fieldNote: He treats **retirement** as a budget question without setting an assumed age.
He would **save new earnings** from extra shifts if full weeks return, separate from existing cash.
His **transition** still needs paid training, an actual place and a posted local bill-covering job.

steps.text: Keep formwork shifts while reviewing retirement costs yearly
Save fixed part of extra-shift pay if full weeks return
Take funded inspection course if actual paid-time place and local job exist
Apply for posted local inspection role if pay covers household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because three years to a capable site robot is short when there is little saved and few nearby jobs. A paid course place, a posted local inspection opening and a crew stop rule would make it possible to act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I can learn a new way to check formwork, but my partner and I still need the old wages while I learn.

portrait: **Felix Kowalski**, 58, leads a formwork gang on building sites and holds a vocational trade certificate.
He and his **partner** have grown children, lower pay, less than one month saved and few similar nearby jobs.
He uses **AI occasionally** for office messages, then checks the wording and keeps structural safety decisions with the crew.
Across faster scenarios, he seeks **worker-led trials** and funded paid-time inspection training tied to a posted local job.
He keeps **retirement open** until household income and bills support a decision, saving from extra shifts if they return.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only about three years before capable robots might take formwork tasks he still needs for wages.
whatWouldHelp: An actual **paid course place**, worker stop rule and posted local inspection role at bill-covering pay would make a move credible.
headlineQuote: I can learn a new way to check formwork, but my partner and I still need the old wages while I learn.
